clue.text: Blithe gal, oddly, is the last to go in pool

definitions.text: the last to go in pool

indicators.note: oddly says the letters of these two words are arranged in a strange new way

explanation.surface: A carefree young woman is apparently the final person to jump into the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pool' looks like a swimming pool, but it is the cue game; 'oddly' is the anagram signal, not a request for odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In pool the black ball numbered eight must be potted last to win the frame.

clue.text: Live in the past? I'd settle Thebes at first

parts.note: ex- describes something former, of the past

indicators.note: at first takes the opening letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A question about whether one could have lived in ancient times, settling the Greek city of Thebes.
explanation.definitionFit: To live is simply to be, to have being: a plain synonym when read as a verb.

clue.text: Look astonished about nothing and explode!

indicators.note: about means going around, so the first word wraps the letter for nothing

parts.note: to gape is to stare open-mouthed in astonishment
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone stares in amazement at nothing in particular and then loses their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means to lose one's temper wildly, an idiomatic sense of blowing up.

clue.text: Go off contrary life coach who bullies one?

indicators.note: contrary means going the opposite way, so the word for going off is read backwards

parts.note: food that goes off will rot
a mentor is an adviser or guide, like a life coach

explanation.surface: A perverse personal coach turns out to be a bully.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who persecutes or bullies another person is their persecutor, so the phrase describes the agent noun.

clue.text: City rising up with weapons can make one thus

indicators.note: in a down clue rising up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
armed means carrying weapons

explanation.surface: An armed uprising in a city would frighten anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the tail phrase: a city rising with weapons would make one frightened, so the clue nearly reads as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Frightened or worried is the state an armed uprising would put a person into.

clue.text: Like husband to get into fish (and whipping)

indicators.note: to get into means these letters go inside the fish's name

parts.note: a ling is a long-bodied sea fish
as can mean like, in the manner of
H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogy

explanation.surface: A man somehow ends up inside a fish, with a whipping thrown in.
explanation.definitionFit: A beating with a whip or lash is a flogging, the same noun sense.

clue.text: Blue party's Michael Gove to his critics?

parts.note: blue means low in spirits, sad
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: How the blue (Conservative) party's Michael Gove is seen by his detractors.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative party, of which Michael Gove was a prominent minister; here it simply means unhappy.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a pathetic, socially inept person, which is the insult critics might throw at a politician.

clue.text: In Mayday message, disheartened recruit types …

indicators.note: In places the following letters inside the distress call

parts.note: SOS is the distress signal, like a Mayday

indicators.note: disheartened means the heart, all the middle letters, is removed, leaving the outside ones

explanation.surface: A dispirited new recruit is mentioned in an emergency distress message.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorts and kinds are both words for categories or varieties of thing.

clue.text: … call God or possibly a band of vicars!

indicators.note: possibly signals that these letters may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Continuing the distress message: call on God, or perhaps on a group of clergymen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like a group of people but is a strip of material worn round the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The stiff white clerical collar is a strip worn round a clergyman's neck.

clue.text: Hot tenor getting angry and tense in a row

indicators.note: a singer getting angry is worked up and stirred, so these letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A heated opera tenor becomes cross and strained during an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a row' suggests a quarrel, but the definition means consecutively.
explanation.definitionFit: British idiom for one after another, consecutively, as in three wins successively.

clue.text: At home, a Right Reverend mixed up 'arse' and 'behind'

parts.note: in means at home
RR is the abbreviation for Right Reverend, a bishop's title

indicators.note: mixed up says the letters of the rude word are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A bishop at home confuses two words for the backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' looks like a rear end, matching 'arse', but it means late with payments.
explanation.definitionFit: Being behind with payments means owing money that is overdue.

clue.text: Clever to ignore Britain's leader? Correct!

indicators.note: to ignore means leave out the following letter

parts.note: bright means clever

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so this takes the opening letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A question of whether it is smart to bypass the British prime minister, answered approvingly.
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation or adjective, it agrees something is accurate or true.

clue.text: Time to have laugh with Hoskins — that's the main idea

parts.note: he, as in he-he, is a laugh
Hoskins is the setter, who refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A setter invites a chuckle with him as the central point of the puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: Crossword setters often refer to themselves by name, so Hoskins gives ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The subject or central topic of a work is its principal idea.

clue.text: Graduate I'd chuck rocks at in town

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate
to stone someone is to throw rocks at them

explanation.surface: A university graduate admits wanting to throw rocks at people in town.
explanation.walkthrough: MAIDSTONE is the county town of Kent in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the county town of Kent, an example of an English town.

clue.text: Son had an online affair, then chilled with drugs

parts.note: to e-date is to conduct a romance over the internet

explanation.surface: A son had an internet romance and then relaxed by taking drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Given a calming drug, a patient is tranquillised into a calm state.

clue.text: Small family: close and very clingy?

parts.note: kin means family
tight means close, as in a close-knit friendship

explanation.surface: A small family that is intimate and very dependent on each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Of clothing, fitting so closely it clings to the body all over.

clue.text: Flipping angry with people, dagnabbit!

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the word for angry is read backwards

parts.note: mad means angry
a nation is a people

explanation.surface: Someone is furious with everyone and swears mildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British oath, fitting the swearing, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of annoyance, the minced American oath standing in for a curse.

clue.text: One walks slowly after essential bit of surgery, I bet

indicators.note: after says the walker comes after the letter from surgery
the essential bit is the very centre, so take the middle letter of the operation word

parts.note: an ambler is someone who walks at a leisurely pace

explanation.surface: A patient shuffling slowly after an operation, offering a confident guess.
explanation.definitionFit: A punter is someone who would say this phrase as they place a wager, so it describes a bettor.

clue.text: Knock about a possible nickname for John Thomas!

definitions.meaning: to knock about is to treat roughly, push and shove

definitions.text: a possible nickname for John Thomas!
definitions.meaning: John Thomas is British slang for the penis, which a man might grip, so a cheeky name for it

explanation.surface: Rough someone up, plus a saucy suggestion for another name for a man's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: John Thomas is old British slang for the penis, from Lady Chatterley's Lover.
explanation.definitionFit: To handle someone roughly is to knock them about; split in two, the words describe a grip on a man.

clue.text: Hoskins is male and said to be wicked

parts.note: the setter Hoskins speaking of himself: I am, contracted
oral means spoken, said aloud

explanation.surface: The setter claims he is a man, rumoured to be a bad lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked and unprincipled conduct is unethical, lacking morals.

clue.text: Principal male child takes for a ride

parts.note: the lead is the principal role or person
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A headmaster's son goes off joyriding.
explanation.definitionFit: Both idioms mean deceiving someone, encouraging false hopes in them.

clue.text: Time to return, then breach undamaged tower

indicators.note: to breach is to break into, so the reversed period goes inside

parts.note: mint means pristine, as in mint condition

indicators.note: to return means going back, so the word for time is written backwards

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A call to come back and break into a tower that is still intact.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender tower on a mosque, from which the call to prayer is made.

clue.text: Do really well to have a bit of a snog

definitions.text: have a bit of a snog
definitions.meaning: snog is British slang for kissing; the phrasal verb is American for kissing and petting

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to succeed or fare well and to kiss and cuddle.

clue.text: Where soldiers might be held up before their division?

definitions.text: Where soldiers might be held up before their division?

parts.words: Where soldiers might be held up before their division?
parts.note: soldiers are strips of toast for dipping in a boiled egg; they stand upright in a rack before being shared out, not troops awaiting their army division

explanation.walkthrough: 'soldiers' are strips of toast in British usage, and 'division' is cutting them up, not an army unit.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand of upright slots holds slices of toast at the breakfast table.

clue.text: Revolutionary group locks up soldiers in boxes?

indicators.note: locks up means holding the soldiers inside
revolutionary means turning round, so the word for group is reversed

parts.note: a set is a group
RE is the Royal Engineers, soldiers

explanation.surface: A rebel group imprisons troops in crates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxes' looks like containers; box is a shrub or tree, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Box is a type of evergreen tree, so boxes are examples of woody plants.

clue.text: Bill gets endless German wine for this purpose only

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a bill or poster

indicators.note: endless means losing the last letter

parts.note: hock is a white wine from the Rhineland

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill takes German wine that never runs out, just for this occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase describes something arranged only for a particular need.

clue.text: Mounting cries of pleasure can create commotion

indicators.note: in a down clue mounting means going upwards, read bottom to top

parts.note: ah and ooh are cries of delight

explanation.surface: Escalating noises of delight can cause a disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuss or uproar; the informal word is a synonym for a commotion.

clue.text: Class of actors heard on the radio

indicators.note: heard on the radio means the word is to be judged by its sound

parts.note: a cast is the group of actors in a production

explanation.surface: A group of performers heard in a radio drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A social rank or hereditary class, especially in Hindu society.

clue.text: Beef's good and ready for eating

parts.note: ripe fruit is ready to eat

explanation.surface: A cut of beef is good and ready to serve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beef' looks like meat but is the slang verb or noun for a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a complaint or grievance.

clue.text: Extract from Sexus: "now drop silky bloomers"

indicators.note: Extract from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A racy quotation from Henry Miller's novel Sexus urging a lover to remove silky underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomers' looks like underwear but means flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Small white flowers of late winter are plants that bloom, hence bloomers.

clue.text: Lover heading west with one's capital abroad

indicators.note: in an across clue heading west means read right to left

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast or lover, as in a fitness nut
one's gives I (one) plus S

explanation.surface: A lover travels west, taking his own fortune overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of Tunisia in North Africa, a foreign capital.

clue.text: After getting excited, tread on me holy place!

indicators.note: after getting excited the letters of these words are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: An excited plea to be stepped on, oddly set in a sacred spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Paris cathedral is a famous example of a sacred building.
